Infrastructure secondaries deal volume has grown at a 28% compound annual rate since 2016, reaching an estimated $US20bn in 2025. 1 Institutional demand continues to build, supported by the asset class's ability to mitigate the J-curve and provide access to seasoned, cash-generative portfolios.

Source: Evercore and Campbell Lutyens data. 2016–2024 from Evercore Full Year 2024 Secondary Market Survey Results; 2025 from Campbell Lutyens FY 2025 Secondary Market Overview Report.

Long-term contractual cash flows, essential-service demand, and inflation-linked revenue mechanisms have historically supported more stable pricing for infrastructure secondaries than other private market segments. Since 2018, annual average pricing has shown a standard deviation of approximately 1.4%, compared with 3.5% for buyout and 8.7% for real estate. 2

Distributions have lagged capital calls since 2016, and available capital remains limited relative to demand. Infrastructure secondaries carry a dry powder ratio of roughly 0.5x annual deal volume, well below the 2.1x seen in infrastructure primaries and a balanced range of 3–4x, suggesting continued selectivity remains available to buyers. 3

Source: MAM internal analysis. Dry powder per Preqin; primaries volume per Pitchbook/Inframation; secondaries volume per Evercore Full Year Secondary Market Review 2024.

Complexity has become the market's defining feature, and the managers who can source it, underwrite it, and structure around it are the ones likely to set the pace for the asset class.

Private capital secondaries have gone from a niche liquidity tool to an asset class in their own right — and within secondaries, infrastructure is the fastest-growing corner of the market. In this episode of Pathways, Daniel McCormack, Macquarie Asset Management's Head of Research, is joined by Wandy Hoh, who co-authored the team's paper on infrastructure secondaries, to unpack why.

Wandy breaks down the numbers behind the boom — a record year for secondaries volume, an infrastructure sub-sector compounding at over 25% annually, and a dry powder ratio that leaves the space meaningfully undercapitalized relative to demand.

From there, the conversation covers how discounts actually work (and why they're not the same as returns), what good underwriting looks like, whether data centres are in bubble territory, and where secondaries fit for both new and mature infrastructure investors.

Welcome to Pathways , a Macquarie Asset Management podcast where we provide fresh perspectives and insights for institutional investors and consultants about real assets, private markets, and macroeconomics.

Private capital secondaries — the buying and selling of stakes in funds and assets that already exist — plays a really important role in private markets. It provides liquidity, but not only that: funds can offer investors a great entry point into high-quality assets. Today, we're going to go a layer deeper and look at infrastructure secondaries in particular. This part of the market has been growing even faster than the overall secondaries market, albeit off a lower base.

Hi everybody, my name's Daniel McCormack. I'm Macquarie Asset Management's Head of Research. Joining me today is Wandy Hoh, who co-authored our team's paper on infrastructure secondaries. We're going to lean on that paper quite heavily in today's discussion, but we'll also talk about what's going on more broadly in the market.

There are three parts to this conversation. First, the market backdrop — why infrastructure secondaries are growing the way they are right now. Second, we're going to dig into the substance of the matter, which is how you find and underwrite good deals — and that's really Wandy's day job, so it's fantastic to have her on the podcast today. Third, we'll look at what all this means for investors in terms of deciding whether and how to allocate to the space.

So, Wandy, welcome to the podcast.

Thank you, Daniel. So great to be here.

Before we get into the detail — in one sentence, why should somebody already investing in infrastructure care about the secondaries market specifically?

If you look at the secondaries market today, it's no longer a workaround or something on the side — it's become a true asset class in itself, and a product in itself, to help investors deploy capital into infrastructure and help investors who are looking for liquidity for their assets access that capital, before the fund life expires.

Great — so let's dig into the market backdrop, and let's start broad. How big is the secondaries market, and how much of that is infrastructure?

If you look at the overall secondaries market, it's been the strongest ever first half in 2026. If we measure it by deal volume, in the first six months — according to Evercore, Lazard, and a bunch of other advisors we track research reports from — the market is at the $120 billion mark in secondaries transaction volume. That's up nearly 20% year on year. This is tremendous growth, and it's not just happening in 2026 — this is the second, third, fourth year we've been seeing this type of growth, and it continues to be the case.

When you look at infrastructure as a sub-sector of that asset class, in the first half of this year we were seeing around $12 billion, year over year. Last year, total deal volume exceeded $20 billion. This year, I think we could possibly go to $30 billion for the full year. So this asset class is actually the highest-compounding sub-sector of secondaries, at roughly an over-25% compound annual growth rate between 2016 and 2025. It's really impressive, and it also speaks to why this asset class is here to stay — an important tool for investors, whether as a buyer or as a seller.

So it's growing faster than the broader secondaries market — that's really interesting. What's driving that strong growth you're seeing, Wandy?

I think there are a couple of things. The first is that, since interest rates increased at the end of 2021, we've seen a few years of DPI decline — historically, that hasn't been the case. If you look at the ten years prior to 2022, you saw DPI at roughly 25% of NAV on an overall, fairly mature portfolio, in distributions per year. That declined to 13% since 2022, and that's been the case as of last year, 2025, as well. I don't think 2026 is shaping up to be any better.

So the first driver is that investors increasingly have to think about portfolio management tools that give them more liquidity — and we're not talking about distressed liquidity here. We're talking about how to manage cash flows so you can deploy into new investments, meet certain obligations, and think about overall portfolio construction. That's really been driving the boom.

But if you look back, this actually makes a lot of sense. Private markets have experienced one of the strongest growth periods since the GFC — in the past ten years, this asset class has grown tremendously. And secondaries always moves in parallel and adjacent to the primary asset class. So the growth in primary markets since the GFC, coupled with the DPI story, coupled with investors thinking more and more about how to best manage their portfolio for efficiency — you're seeing very strong growth in secondaries as a result.

Yeah, that's fascinating — and that's the supply side. What about the demand side? Is there enough capital chasing all of this?
